q.s: A 36-week fetus has bilateral hydronephrosis, a distended thick-walled bladder and severe oligohydramnios on ultrasound. The fetus is male. After birth, he has a weak urinary stream, flattened facial features and respiratory distress.
e: Wrong. No kidneys or bladder distension.
Correct. Most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in male infants.
Wrong. Enlarged echogenic kidneys, no bladder distension.
Wrong. Not the cause of oligohydramnios here.
cl: Low fetal urine output reaching amniotic fluid.
q.ch: Male fetus + bilateral hydronephrosis + thick bladder + oligohydramnios → posterior urethral valves → Potter features.
q.tr: Pulmonary hypoplasia is the main cause of death in Potter sequence.
q.q2: What is the most likely cause?

q.s: A 15-year-old girl with short stature and a webbed neck has recurrent urinary tract infections. CT shows both kidneys joined at their lower poles, lying lower than normal in front of the aorta.
cl: short stature and a webbed neck
q.ch: Turner syndrome + fused inferior poles + low kidneys → horseshoe kidney trapped by IMA.
q.tr: Associated with UPJ obstruction, stones, infection and renal cancer.
q.q2: Which vessel prevented the kidneys from ascending?

q.s: A 30-year-old woman has a hysterectomy for fibroids. Two days later she has flank pain and fever. CT shows hydronephrosis on the left with a dilated ureter down to the level of the uterine artery ligation.
o: It runs with the round ligament
It passes over the common iliac artery
It passes over the uterine artery
It lies inside the bladder wall
It passes through the broad ligament above the ovary
It passes under the uterine artery near the cervix
e: Wrong. True but not the injury site here.
cl: down to the level of the uterine artery ligation
q.ch: Hysterectomy + hydronephrosis to uterine artery level → ureter ligated where it passes under the uterine artery.
q.tr: In men, the ureter passes under the vas deferens.
q.q2: Why was this structure injured?
q.fc: Results from a renal clearance study

q.s: A healthy volunteer has a renal clearance study. The results are shown.
q.ch: Inulin clearance = GFR (120 mL/min); PAH clearance = eRPF (600 mL/min) → FF = 20%.
q.tr: RBF = RPF/(1 − Hct) = 1000 mL/min.
q.q2: What is the filtration fraction?

q.s: A 78-year-old woman with heart failure takes lisinopril and furosemide. She starts taking naproxen for knee pain. A week later her creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL.
o: No arteriolar change; tubular toxicity only
Afferent constriction (NSAID) and efferent dilation (ACE inhibitor)
cl: creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL
q.ch: NSAID blocks prostaglandin afferent dilation + ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction + diuretic volume loss → falling glomerular pressure → AKI ("triple whammy").
q.tr: Prostaglandins dilate afferent (PDA); angiotensin II constricts efferent (ACE).
q.q2: What happened to her glomerular arterioles?
q.fc: Renal handling of glucose in a healthy adult

q.s: A medical student studies the curves shown, which describe glucose handling in a healthy adult. Glucose first appears in the urine at about 200 mg/dL, yet the reabsorption curve does not reach its plateau until about 375 mg/min.
o: Glucose is filtered less at high concentrations
Glucose is secreted at high levels
cl: first appears in the urine at about 200 mg/dL
does not reach its plateau until about 375 mg/min
glucose handling in a healthy adult
q.ch: Threshold (~200 mg/dL) to Tm (~375 mg/min) region = splay from nephron heterogeneity.
q.tr: Pregnancy and SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria below the normal threshold.
q.q2: What explains the gradual rather than sharp transition?

q.s: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes starts a new oral drug. His HbA1c falls, he loses 2 kg and his urine dipstick is strongly positive for glucose even when his blood glucose is 130 mg/dL. He also develops balanitis.
cl: urine dipstick is strongly positive for glucose
q.ch: Glucosuria at normal glucose + weight loss + genital infection → SGLT2 inhibitor → PCT.
q.tr: SGLT2 reabsorbs most filtered glucose in the early PCT.
q.q2: Where does the drug act?
q.fc: Tubular fluid-to-plasma concentration ratios along the proximal tubule; dashed line = ratio of 1

q.s: A physiologist measures three substances along the proximal tubule. The results are shown. Substance X is freely filtered and its total amount in the tubule does not change.
o: X = inulin, Y = sodium, Z = glucose
X = bicarbonate, Y = urea, Z = PAH
X = PAH, Y = glucose, Z = sodium
X = sodium, Y = glucose, Z = inulin
X = glucose, Y = inulin, Z = sodium
X = glucose, Y = sodium, Z = inulin
cl: freely filtered and its total amount in the tubule does not change
three substances along the proximal tubule
q.ch: Concentration rises as water leaves (inulin); stays at 1 with isotonic reabsorption (Na+); falls toward 0 when reabsorbed faster than water (glucose).
q.tr: PAH rises even more than inulin because it is secreted.
q.q2: Which substances are X, Y and Z?
q.fc: Findings in two young adults who take no medications

q.s: Two young adults are evaluated for weakness and muscle cramps. Neither uses diuretics or laxatives. Their findings are shown.
o: Na+/Cl− cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Epithelial Na+ channel in the collecting tubule
Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
q.ch: Normotensive hypokalemic alkalosis + low Mg2+ + low urine Ca2+ → Gitelman (thiazide-like DCT defect); high urine Ca2+ → Bartter (loop-like).
q.tr: Gitelman is milder than Bartter.
q.q2: Which transporter is defective in patient 2?

q.s: A 19-year-old man has a BP of 172/104 mm Hg. Serum K+ is 2.9 mEq/L and HCO3− is 31 mEq/L. Plasma renin and aldosterone are both very low. His mother and brother also have hypertension starting in adolescence. He does not eat licorice.
cl: Serum K+ is 2.9 mEq/L and HCO3− is 31 mEq/L
renin and aldosterone are both very low
q.ch: Young hypertensive + hypokalemic alkalosis + low renin/aldosterone + AD inheritance → Liddle syndrome → amiloride.
q.tr: AME also has low renin and aldosterone but is recessive or from licorice.
q.q2: Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?

q.s: A 70-year-old woman with heart failure takes high doses of furosemide. Her ECG shows flattened T waves and prominent U waves. She reports leg cramps.
e: Correct. Loop diuretics waste Mg2+ and K+.
cl: flattened T waves and prominent U waves
q.ch: Loop diuretic → loss of K+ and Mg2+ (OHH DAANG) → hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia.
q.tr: Correct magnesium first, or potassium will not stay up.
q.q2: Which other finding is most likely?
q.fc: Arterial blood gas and serum chemistry

q.s: A 17-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain and deep, rapid breathing after missing insulin doses. Her results are shown.
o: Normal anion gap acidosis with respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis with concomitant respiratory acidosis
Elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Normal anion gap acidosis from diarrhea
q.ch: DKA → anion gap 134 − (98 + 8) = 28 → AG metabolic acidosis; Winters predicts PCO2 18–22 → appropriately compensated.
q.tr: Ketones are the K in GOLDMARK.
q.q2: Which statement best describes her acid-base status?

q.s: A 45-year-old man is found confused after a party. He has an elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis, an elevated osmolal gap and envelope-shaped crystals in his urine. Creatinine is rising.
e: Wrong. Visual loss, no oxalate crystals.
q.ch: AG acidosis + osmolal gap + oxalate crystals + AKI → ethylene glycol (antifreeze).
q.tr: Treat with fomepizole.
q.q2: What did he ingest?

q.s: A 24-year-old woman has had severe watery diarrhea for 5 days from a cholera-like illness. Arterial pH is 7.30, HCO3− is 15 mEq/L, Na+ is 138 mEq/L and Cl− is 113 mEq/L.
o: 10 mEq/L; normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
q.ch: Diarrhea → HCO3− loss with Cl− retention → normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis (SHARDS).
q.tr: Normal anion gap is about 8–12 mEq/L.
q.q2: What is the anion gap and its category?

q.s: A 27-year-old woman with Sjögren syndrome has recurrent kidney stones. She has a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia and a urine pH of 6.5. The stones are radiopaque and composed of calcium phosphate.
o: Defective HCO3− reabsorption in the PCT
Defective NaCl transport in the DCT
e: Wrong. Type 2; urine pH can drop below 5.5.
q.ch: Autoimmune disease + NAGMA + hypokalemia + urine pH > 5.5 + CaP stones → distal RTA.
q.tr: Amphotericin B also causes type 1 RTA.
q.q2: Which defect is present?

q.s: A 62-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes and CKD has a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Serum K+ is 6.1 mEq/L. Renin and aldosterone are low. He takes lisinopril.
o: Uremic acidosis with high anion gap
e: Correct. Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism worsened by ACE inhibitor.
q.ch: Diabetes + NAGMA + hyperkalemia + low aldosterone → type 4 RTA (↓ NH3 synthesis).
q.tr: Hyperkalemia itself suppresses ammoniagenesis.
q.q2: Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present?

q.s: An 8-year-old boy has smoky brown urine and puffy eyes. Three weeks ago he had impetigo on his legs. His BP is 142/92 mm Hg. Urine shows RBC casts and mild proteinuria. Serum C3 is low.
cl: smoky brown urine and puffy eyes
Three weeks ago he had impetigo
Latent period after streptococcal skin infection.
q.ch: Strep infection 2–4 weeks earlier + nephritic syndrome + low C3 → PSGN → subepithelial humps.
q.tr: IgA nephropathy occurs during the infection, with normal complement.
q.q2: What would electron microscopy of a kidney biopsy show?

q.s: A 23-year-old man coughs up blood and has rapidly rising creatinine over 2 weeks. Urine has RBC casts. Kidney biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli with smooth linear IgG along the basement membrane.
o: Autoantibodies against type IV collagen in basement membranes (type II hypersensitivity)
q.ch: Hemoptysis + RPGN + linear IgG → anti-GBM (Goodpasture) → type II hypersensitivity.
q.tr: Treat urgently with plasmapheresis, steroids and cyclophosphamide.
q.q2: What is the mechanism of his disease?

q.s: A 47-year-old man has chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal discharge, cough with lung nodules on CT and hematuria with RBC casts. Kidney biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with no immune deposits on immunofluorescence.
cl: chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal discharge
q.ch: Upper airway + lung nodules + pauci-immune crescentic GN → GPA → PR3-ANCA.
q.tr: MPA has p-ANCA and no granulomas; EGPA adds asthma and eosinophilia.
q.q2: Which antibody is most likely positive?

q.s: A 16-year-old boy has persistent microscopic hematuria. He wears hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss. Eye exam shows a cone-shaped bulging of the lens. His maternal uncle had kidney failure at 30.
o: Irregular thickening and splitting of the GBM with a basket-weave pattern
q.ch: Hematuria + hearing loss + lens abnormality + X-linked → Alport (type IV collagen) → basket-weave GBM.
q.tr: "Can't see, can't pee, can't hear a bee."
q.q2: What would electron microscopy of the kidney show?

head: Test
Result
Reference
rows: Oval fat bodies; no RBC casts

q.s: A 56-year-old man has had leg swelling and frothy urine for 2 months. He now has left flank pain and gross hematuria, and a CT shows a clot in the left renal vein. His earlier results are shown.
o: Effacement of foot processes with normal GBM
cl: clot in the left renal vein
q.ch: Adult nephrotic syndrome + anti-PLA2R + renal vein thrombosis → primary membranous nephropathy → spike-and-dome.
q.tr: Secondary causes include drugs, HBV/HCV, SLE and solid tumors.
q.q2: What would electron microscopy of his kidney biopsy show?

q.s: A 4-year-old boy has puffy eyes and swollen legs 10 days after an upper respiratory infection. Urine protein is 4+ with no blood. His BP is normal. He responds completely to prednisone.
o: Normal light microscopy and effaced podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy
cl: 10 days after an upper respiratory infection
Urine protein is 4+ with no blood
q.ch: Child + nephrotic syndrome after infection + steroid response → minimal change disease.
q.tr: Rarely secondary to Hodgkin lymphoma.
q.q2: Which finding would be seen on kidney biopsy if it were done?

q.s: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 30 years has increasing leg edema. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is markedly elevated. Kidney biopsy shows round, eosinophilic nodules in the mesangium.
e: Wrong. Not renoprotective in the same way.
cl: round, eosinophilic nodules in the mesangium
q.ch: Long diabetes + albuminuria + nodular glomerulosclerosis → diabetic nephropathy → ACE inhibitor/ARB.
q.tr: Most common cause of ESRD in the US.
q.q2: Which drug class slows progression of her kidney disease?

q.s: A 35-year-old man has sudden severe left flank pain that radiates to his groin, with nausea and hematuria. Plain x-ray shows no stone, but CT shows a 6-mm stone at the ureterovesical junction. He has gout. Urine pH is 5.0.
q.ch: Radiolucent stone + gout + acidic urine → uric acid stone → alkalinize urine, allopurinol.
q.tr: "I can't see you": cystine and uric acid are radiolucent.
q.q2: What prevents recurrence of this type of stone?

q.s: A 54-year-old woman with a long-term urinary catheter has fever and flank pain. CT shows a large branching stone filling the right renal pelvis and calyces. Urine pH is 8.5, and urine culture grows Proteus mirabilis.
q.ch: Urease-positive infection → urea → NH3 → alkaline urine → struvite staghorn.
q.tr: Treat the infection and remove the stone surgically.
q.q2: What is the composition of the stone?

q.s: A 72-year-old woman is admitted with pneumonia and septic shock. Her BP was 70/40 mm Hg for 6 hours before resuscitation. Two days later her creatinine is 3.8 mg/dL. Urine Na+ is 62 mEq/L, FENa is 4% and urine microscopy shows many muddy brown granular casts.
o: Proximal tubule and thick ascending limb in the outer medulla
cl: BP was 70/40 mm Hg for 6 hours
q.ch: Prolonged hypotension + FENa > 2% + muddy brown casts → ischemic ATN → PT and TAL.
q.tr: The medulla receives much less blood flow than the cortex.
q.q2: Which renal regions are most susceptible to this injury?
q.fc: Urine and serum indices in two patients with acute kidney injury

q.s: Two patients have acute kidney injury. Patient 1 has had severe vomiting for 3 days. Patient 2 received IV contrast and gentamicin. Their results are shown.
o: Increased urea production from tissue breakdown
Low renal blood flow increases tubular reabsorption of Na+, water and urea
cl: Two patients have acute kidney injury
q.ch: Prerenal: concentrated urine, low Na+, FENa < 1%, BUN/Cr > 20; ATN: dilute urine, high Na+, FENa > 2%, BUN/Cr < 15.
q.tr: Diuretics can falsely raise FENa in prerenal states.
q.q2: Why is patient 1's BUN-to-creatinine ratio high?

q.s: A 64-year-old man started amoxicillin 10 days ago for sinusitis. He now has fever, a diffuse itchy rash and a creatinine of 2.9 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows white cells and white cell casts. A special stain shows eosinophils in the urine.
q.ch: Penicillin + fever + rash + WBC casts + eosinophiluria → AIN → stop drug.
q.tr: DRAINS: Diuretics, Rifampin, Antibiotics, PPIs, NSAIDs, Sulfa drugs.
q.q2: What is the most appropriate next step?

q.s: A 70-year-old man with CKD stage 5 has missed two dialysis sessions. His ECG shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS. Serum K+ is 7.4 mEq/L.
e: Correct. Stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes.
Wrong. Shifts K+, but not the fastest protection.
cl: tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS
q.ch: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes → IV calcium first, then shift K+ (insulin, β2-agonist), then remove (dialysis).
q.tr: Insulin and β-agonists shift K+ into cells.
q.q2: Which treatment acts fastest to protect his heart?

q.s: A 66-year-old man on hemodialysis has bone pain. His serum calcium is 7.9 mg/dL, phosphate 7.8 mg/dL and PTH 860 pg/mL. X-rays show subperiosteal bone resorption of the fingers.
o: Phosphate retention and reduced calcitriol synthesis causing hypocalcemia
q.ch: ESRD → phosphate retention + ↓ 1α-hydroxylation → hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism → renal osteodystrophy.
q.tr: If PTH becomes autonomous with hypercalcemia: tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
q.q2: What is the primary mechanism of his elevated PTH?

q.s: A 42-year-old man has hypertension, intermittent flank pain and hematuria. Both kidneys are enlarged and palpable. Ultrasound shows many cysts in both kidneys and a few in the liver. His father died of a subarachnoid hemorrhage at age 50.
cl: Both kidneys are enlarged and palpable
many cysts in both kidneys and a few in the liver
q.ch: Adult bilateral enlarged cystic kidneys + liver cysts + family SAH → ADPKD → PKD1 (chromosome 16).
q.tr: Also associated with mitral valve prolapse and diverticulosis.
q.q2: Which gene is most likely mutated?

head: Measurement
Result
rows: Bruit in the right upper quadrant

q.s: A 71-year-old man who has smoked for 50 years has hypertension that remains uncontrolled on three drugs. He has peripheral artery disease. His findings are shown.
o: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the distal left renal artery
Atherosclerotic stenosis of the proximal right renal artery
e: Wrong. Renin would be low on both sides.
q.ch: Older smoker + resistant HTN + small right kidney + high right renin + bruit → atherosclerotic right renal artery stenosis.
q.tr: FMD affects young women in the distal two-thirds of the renal artery.
q.q2: What is the most likely cause, and where is the lesion?

q.s: A 64-year-old male smoker has flank pain, a palpable left flank mass and blood in his urine. He also has new swelling of veins around his left testicle that does not collapse when he lies down. His hemoglobin is 18.6 g/dL.
o: It arises from the collecting duct
It arises from the proximal tubule and is linked to chromosome 3 deletions
It is associated with chromosome 11 deletion
e: Correct. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
cl: flank pain, a palpable left flank mass and blood in his urine
does not collapse when he lies down
q.ch: Classic triad + left varicocele + polycythemia → RCC → PCT origin, chromosome 3 (VHL).
q.tr: Paraneoplastic "PEAR": PTHrP, EPO, ACTH, Renin.
q.q2: Which statement about his tumor is correct?

q.s: A 3-year-old girl's mother notices a large, firm, smooth mass on the right side of her abdomen while bathing her. It does not cross the midline. The girl has no iris in either eye and has delayed development.
e: Correct. WT1 deletion in WAGR complex.
cl: It does not cross the midline
q.ch: Toddler + unilateral flank mass + aniridia + developmental delay → WAGR → Wilms tumor (WT1, chromosome 11).
q.tr: Beckwith-Wiedemann is linked to WT2.
q.q2: Which chromosome is affected?

q.s: A 66-year-old retired dye factory worker who smoked for 40 years has painless gross hematuria. Urine has no casts. Cystoscopy shows a papillary mass in the bladder.
q.ch: Smoking + aromatic amines + painless hematuria → urothelial carcinoma ("Pee SAC").
q.tr: Cyclophosphamide also increases the risk.
q.q2: What is the most likely tumor type?

q.s: A 28-year-old climber is planning a trip to 5000 m. He is prescribed a drug to start 1 day before the ascent. A week later he notices tingling in his fingers and soda tastes flat.
o: It inhibits carbonic anhydrase, causing a metabolic acidosis that stimulates breathing
q.ch: Altitude prophylaxis + paresthesias → acetazolamide → HCO3− diuresis → metabolic acidosis offsets respiratory alkalosis.
q.tr: Also used for glaucoma and IIH; causes type 2 RTA.
q.q2: How does the drug help prevent altitude sickness?

q.s: A 50-year-old woman with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones has a 24-hour urine calcium that is high. Serum calcium and PTH are normal.
cl: Serum calcium and PTH are normal
q.ch: Idiopathic hypercalciuria with calcium stones → thiazide → ↓ urine calcium.
q.tr: Citrate and a low-sodium diet also help.
q.q2: Which drug reduces her urine calcium?

q.s: A 30-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on lithium has polyuria of 6 L/day with a urine osmolality of 120 mOsm/kg. Desmopressin does not concentrate her urine. Her psychiatrist wants to keep lithium.
e: Wrong. Treats DI but raises lithium levels.
Correct. Blocks ENaC through which lithium enters principal cells.
cl: Desmopressin does not concentrate her urine
q.ch: Lithium-induced nephrogenic DI → amiloride blocks ENaC (lithium entry) and reduces polyuria.
q.tr: Thiazides also treat nephrogenic DI but raise lithium levels.
q.q2: Which drug both treats her polyuria and reduces lithium entry into collecting duct cells?

q.s: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and bilateral renal artery stenosis is started on ramipril. Within a week, his creatinine rises from 1.3 to 2.8 mg/dL and his potassium is 5.9 mEq/L.
o: Loss of angiotensin II–mediated efferent constriction, which was maintaining GFR
q.ch: Bilateral RAS → GFR maintained by angiotensin II efferent constriction → ACE inhibitor removes it → AKI + hyperkalemia.
q.tr: ARBs and aliskiren have the same risk.
q.q2: What is the mechanism of his AKI?

q.s: A 9-year-old boy with cystinosis has excessive thirst and urination, poor growth and bowed legs. Urine shows glucose with a normal blood glucose, amino acids and phosphate. Blood shows a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia.
o: Loop of Henle; vitamin D excess
Proximal convoluted tubule; urinary phosphate loss causes rickets
Thick ascending limb; calcium loss causes rickets
cl: glucose with a normal blood glucose
non-anion gap metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia
q.ch: Glucosuria + aminoaciduria + phosphaturia + proximal RTA → Fanconi syndrome → hypophosphatemic rickets.
q.tr: Causes include Wilson disease, tyrosinemia, myeloma, ifosfamide, tenofovir and lead.
q.q2: Which nephron segment is affected, and why are his legs bowed?
